{{Short description|Mathematical term}}
In [[mathematics]], in particular in [[algebraic geometry]] and [[differential geometry]], '''Dolbeault cohomology''' (named after [[Pierre Dolbeault]]) is an analog of [[de Rham cohomology]] for [[complex manifold]]s.  Let ''M'' be a complex manifold.  Then the Dolbeault cohomology groups <math>H^{p,q}(M, \Complex)</math> depend on a pair of integers ''p'' and ''q'' and are realized as a [[subquotient]] of the space of [[complex differential form]]s of degree (''p'',''q'').

==Construction of the cohomology groups==
Let <math>\Omega^{p,q}</math> be the [[vector bundle]] of complex differential forms of degree <math>(p,q)</math>. In the article on [[complex differential form|complex forms]], the Dolbeault operator is defined as a [[differential operator]] on smooth sections

:<math>\bar{\partial}:\Omega^{p,q}\to\Omega^{p,q+1}.</math>

Since <math>\bar{\partial}^2=0</math>, this operator has some associated [[cohomology]].  Specifically, define the cohomology to be the [[quotient space (linear algebra)|quotient space]]

:<math>H^{p,q}(M,\Complex)=\frac {\ker\,(\bar \partial: \Omega^{p,q} \to \Omega^{p,q+1})}{\mathrm{im}\, (\bar \partial : \Omega^{p,q-1} \to \Omega^{p,q})}.</math>

==Dolbeault cohomology of vector bundles==

If ''E'' is a [[holomorphic vector bundle]] on a complex manifold ''X'', then one can define likewise a fine [[injective resolution|resolution]] of the [[Sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]] <math>\mathcal O(E)</math> of holomorphic sections of ''E'', using the [[Holomorphic_vector_bundle#Dolbeault_operators|Dolbeault operator]] of ''E''. This is therefore a resolution of the [[sheaf cohomology]] of <math>\mathcal O(E)</math>. 

In particular associated to the holomorphic structure of <math>E</math> is a Dolbeault operator <math>\bar \partial_E : \Gamma(E) \to \Omega^{0,1}(E)</math> taking sections of <math>E</math> to <math>(0,1)</math>-forms with values in <math>E</math>. This satisfies the characteristic [[Product rule|Leibniz rule]] with respect to the Dolbeault operator <math>\bar \partial</math> on differential forms, and is therefore sometimes known as a '''<math>(0,1)</math>-connection''' on <math>E</math>, Therefore, in the same way that a connection on a vector bundle can be extended to the [[exterior covariant derivative]], the Dolbeault operator of <math>E</math> can be extended to an operator

<math display="block">\bar \partial_E : \Omega^{p,q}(E) \to \Omega^{p,q+1}(E)</math>which acts on a section <math>\alpha \otimes s \in \Omega^{p,q}(E)</math> by

<math display="block">\bar \partial_E (\alpha \otimes s) = (\bar \partial \alpha) \otimes s + (-1)^{p+q} \alpha \wedge \bar \partial_E s</math>and is extended linearly to any section in <math>\Omega^{p,q}(E)</math>. The Dolbeault operator satisfies the integrability condition <math>\bar \partial_E ^2 = 0</math> and so '''Dolbeault cohomology with coefficients in''' <math>E</math> can be defined as above:

<math display="block">H^{p,q}(X,(E,\bar \partial_E)) = \frac {\ker\,(\bar \partial_E: \Omega^{p,q}(E) \to \Omega^{p,q+1}(E))}{\mathrm{im}\, (\bar \partial_E : \Omega^{p,q-1}(E) \to \Omega^{p,q}(E))}.</math>The Dolbeault cohomology groups do not depend on the choice of Dolbeault operator <math>\bar \partial_E</math> compatible with the holomorphic structure of <math>E</math>, so are typically denoted by <math>H^{p,q}(X,E)</math> dropping the dependence on <math>\bar \partial_E</math>.

== Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma ==
In order to establish the Dolbeault isomorphism we need to prove the '''Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma''' (or '''<math>\bar{\partial}</math>-[[Poincaré lemma]]'''). First we prove a one-dimensional version of the <math>\bar{\partial}</math>-Poincaré lemma; we shall use the following generalised form of the [[Cauchy's integral formula#Smooth functions|Cauchy integral representation for smooth functions]]:

'''Proposition''': Let <math>B_{\varepsilon}(0):=\lbrace z\in\Complex \mid | z|<\varepsilon\rbrace</math> the open ball centered in <math>0</math> of radius <math>\varepsilon\in\R _{>0},</math> <math>\overline{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\subseteq U</math> open and <math>f\in\mathcal{C}^\infty(U)</math>, then 

:<math>\forall z\in B_{\varepsilon}(0): \quad f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\partial B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{f(\xi)}{\xi-z}d\xi+\frac{1}{2\pi i}\iint_{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\bar{\xi}}\frac{d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}}{\xi-z}.</math>

'''Lemma''' (<math>\bar{\partial}</math>-Poincaré lemma on the [[complex plane]]): Let <math>B_{\varepsilon}(0),U</math> be as before and <math>\alpha=f d\bar{z}\in\mathcal{A}^{0,1}_{\Complex}(U)</math> a smooth form, then
:<math>\mathcal{C}^\infty(U)\ni g(z):=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{f(\xi)}{\xi-z}d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}</math> 
satisfies <math>\alpha=\bar{\partial}g</math> on <math>B_{\varepsilon}(0).</math>

''Proof.'' Our claim is that <math>g</math> defined above is a well-defined smooth function and <math>\alpha = f\, d\bar{z} = \bar{\partial} g</math>. To show this we choose a point <math>z\in B_{\varepsilon}(0)</math> and an open neighbourhood <math>z\in V\subseteq B_{\varepsilon}(0)</math>, then we can find a smooth function <math>\rho: B_{\varepsilon}(0)\to\R </math> whose support is compact and lies in <math>B_{\varepsilon}(0)</math> and <math>\rho|_V\equiv 1.</math> Then we can write 

:<math>f=f_1+f_2:=\rho f+(1-\rho)f</math> 

and define

:<math> g_i:=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{f_i(\xi)}{\xi-z}d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}.</math>

Since <math> f_2\equiv 0</math> in <math>V</math> then <math>g_2</math> is clearly well-defined and smooth; we note that

:<math>\begin{align}  
g_1&=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{f_1(\xi)}{\xi-z}d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}\\
   &=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\Complex}\frac{f_1(\xi)}{\xi-z}d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}\\
   &=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\infty\int_0^{2\pi}f_1(z+re^{i\theta})e^{-i\theta}d\theta dr,
\end{align}</math>

which is indeed well-defined and smooth, therefore the same is true for <math>g</math>. Now we show that <math>\bar{\partial}g=\alpha</math> on <math>B_{\varepsilon}(0)</math>.

:<math>\frac{\partial g_2}{\partial\bar{z}}=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}f_2(\xi)\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{z}}\Big(\frac{1}{\xi-z}\Big)d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}=0</math>

since <math>(\xi-z)^{-1}</math> is holomorphic in <math>B_{\varepsilon}(0)\setminus V</math> .

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{\partial g_1}{\partial \bar{z}}=&\pi^{-1}\int_{\Complex}\frac{\partial f_1(z+re^{i\theta})}{\partial\bar{z}} e^{-i\theta}d\theta\wedge dr\\
=& \pi^{-1}\int_{\Complex }\Big(\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial\bar{z}}\Big)(z+re^{i\theta}) e^{-i\theta}d\theta\wedge dr\\
=&\frac{1}{2\pi i}\iint_{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial\bar{\xi}}\frac{d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}}{\xi-z}
\end{align}</math>

applying the generalised Cauchy formula to <math>f_1</math> we find

:<math>f_1(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\partial B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{f_1(\xi)}{\xi-z}d\xi+\frac{1}{2\pi i}\iint_{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial\bar{\xi}}\frac{d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}}{\xi-z} =\frac{1}{2\pi i}\iint_{B_{\varepsilon}(0)}\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial\bar{\xi}}\frac{d\xi\wedge d\bar{\xi}}{\xi-z}</math>

since <math>f_1|_{\partial B_{\varepsilon}(0)}=0</math>, but then <math>f=f_1=\frac{\partial g_1}{\partial\bar{z}}=\frac{\partial g}{\partial\bar{z}}</math> on <math> V</math>. Since <math>z</math> was arbitrary, the lemma is now proved. 

===Proof of Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma===

Now are ready to prove the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma; the proof presented here is due to [[Grothendieck]].<ref>{{citation|last=Serre|first=Jean-Pierre|authorlink=Jean-Pierre Serre|title=Faisceaux analytiques sur l'espace projectif|journal=Séminaire Henri Cartan|volume= 6|year=1953–1954|issue=Talk no. 18|pages=1–10|
url=http://www.numdam.org/item?id=SHC_1953-1954__6__A18_0}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511629327.002|chapter=Calculus on Complex Manifolds |title=Several Complex Variables and Complex Manifolds II |year=1982 |pages=1–64 |isbn=9780521288880 }}</ref> We denote with <math>\Delta_{\varepsilon}^n(0)</math> the open [[polydisc]] centered in <math>0\in\Complex^n</math> with radius <math>\varepsilon\in\R_{>0}</math>.

'''Lemma''' (Dolbeault–Grothendieck): Let <math>\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex^n}^{p,q}(U)</math> where <math>\overline{\Delta_{\varepsilon}^n(0)} \subseteq U</math> open and <math>q>0</math> such that <math>\bar{\partial}\alpha=0</math>, then there exists <math>\beta\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex^n}^{p,q-1}(U)</math> which satisfies: <math>\alpha=\bar{\partial}\beta</math> on <math>\Delta_{\varepsilon}^n(0).</math>

Before starting the proof we note that any <math>(p,q)</math>-form can be written as

:<math> \alpha=\sum_{IJ}\alpha_{IJ} dz_I\wedge d\bar{z}_J=\sum_{J}\left(\sum_I\alpha_{IJ} dz_I\right)_J\wedge d\bar{z}_J</math>

for multi-indices <math>I,J,|I|=p,|J|=q</math>, therefore we can reduce the proof to the case <math>\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex ^n}^{0,q}(U)</math>.

''Proof.'' Let <math>k>0</math> be the smallest index such that <math>\alpha\in(d\bar{z}_1,\dots,d\bar{z}_k)</math> in the sheaf of <math>\mathcal{C}^\infty</math>-modules, we proceed by induction on <math>k</math>. For <math>k=0</math> we have <math>\alpha\equiv0</math> since <math>q>0</math>; next we suppose that if <math>\alpha\in(d\bar{z}_1,\dots,d\bar{z}_k)</math> then there exists <math>\beta\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex^n}^{0,q-1}(U)</math> such that <math>\alpha=\bar{\partial}\beta</math> on <math>\Delta_{\varepsilon}^n(0)</math>. Then suppose <math>\omega \in (d\bar{z}_1, \dots, d\bar{z}_{k+1})</math> and observe that we can write

:<math>\omega=d\bar{z}_{k+1}\wedge \psi + \mu, \qquad \psi, \mu\in(d\bar{z}_1,\dots,d\bar{z}_k).</math>

Since <math>\omega</math> is <math>\bar{\partial}</math>-closed it follows that <math>\psi, \mu</math> are holomorphic in variables <math>z_{k+2},\dots,z_n</math> and smooth in the remaining ones on the polydisc <math>\Delta_{\varepsilon}^n(0)</math>. Moreover we can apply the <math>\bar{\partial}</math>-Poincaré lemma to the smooth functions <math>z_{k+1} \mapsto \psi_J(z_1, \dots,z_{k+1}, \dots, z_n)</math> on the open ball <math>B_{\varepsilon_{k+1}}(0)</math>, hence there exist a family of smooth functions <math>g_J</math> which satisfy 

:<math>\psi_J=\frac{\partial g_J}{\partial\bar{z}_{k+1}}\quad \text{on} \quad B_{\varepsilon_{k+1}}(0).</math>

<math>g_J</math> are also holomorphic in <math>z_{k+2},\dots,z_n</math>. Define 

:<math>\tilde{\psi}:=\sum_J g_J d\bar{z}_{J}</math> 

then

:<math>\begin{align}
\omega-\bar{\partial}\tilde{\psi}&=d\bar{z}_{k+1}\wedge\psi +\mu-\sum_J\frac{\partial g_J}{\partial\bar{z}_{k+1}}d\bar{z}_{k+1}\wedge d\bar{z}_J +\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_J\frac{\partial g_J}{\partial \bar{z}_{j}}d\bar{z}_j\wedge d\bar{z}_{J\setminus\lbrace j\rbrace}\\
&=d\bar{z}_{k+1}\wedge\psi+\mu-d\bar{z}_{k+1}\wedge\psi+\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_J\frac{\partial g_J}{\partial \bar{z}_{j}}d\bar{z}_j\wedge d\bar{z}_{J\setminus\lbrace j\rbrace}\\
&=\mu+\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_J\frac{\partial g_J}{\partial\bar{z}_{j}}d\bar{z}_j\wedge d\bar{z}_{J\setminus\lbrace j \rbrace} \in (d\bar{z}_1, \dots, d\bar{z}_{k}),
\end{align}</math>

therefore we can apply the induction hypothesis to it, there exists <math>\eta\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex ^n}^{0,q-1}(U)</math> such that

:<math>\omega-\bar{\partial}\tilde{\psi}=\bar{\partial}\eta \quad \text{on} \quad \Delta_{\varepsilon}^n(0)</math>

and <math>\zeta:=\eta+\tilde{\psi}</math> ends the induction step. QED

:The previous lemma can be generalised by admitting polydiscs with <math>\varepsilon_k=+\infty</math> for some of the components of the polyradius.

'''Lemma''' (extended Dolbeault-Grothendieck). If <math>\Delta_\varepsilon^n(0)</math> is an open polydisc with <math>\varepsilon_k\in\R \cup \lbrace +\infty \rbrace </math> and <math>q>0</math>, then <math>H^{p,q}_{\bar{\partial}}(\Delta_\varepsilon^n(0))=0.</math>

''Proof.'' We consider two cases: <math>\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex^n}^{p,q+1}(U), q>0</math> and <math>\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex^n}^{p,1}(U)</math>.

<u>Case 1.</u> Let <math>\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex^n}^{p,q+1}(U), q>0</math>, and we cover <math>\Delta_\varepsilon^n(0)</math> with polydiscs <math>\overline{\Delta_i} \subset\Delta_{i+1}</math>, then by the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma we can find forms <math>\beta_i</math> of bidegree <math>(p,q-1)</math> on <math>\overline{\Delta_i}\subseteq U_i</math> open such that <math>\alpha |_{\Delta_i} = \bar{\partial} \beta_i</math>; we want to show that 

:<math>\beta_{i+1}|_{\Delta_i}=\beta_i.</math>

We proceed by induction on <math>i</math>: the case when <math>i=1</math> holds by the previous lemma. Let the claim be true for <math>k>1</math> and take <math>\Delta_{k+1}</math> with 

:<math>\Delta_{\varepsilon}^n(0)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k+1}\Delta_i \quad \text{and} \quad \overline{\Delta_k}\subset\Delta_{k+1}.</math>

Then we find a <math>(p,q-1)</math>-form <math>\beta'_{k+1}</math> defined in an open neighbourhood of <math>\overline{\Delta_{k+1}}</math> such that <math>\alpha|_{\Delta_{k+1}}=\bar{\partial}\beta_{k+1}</math>. Let <math>U_k</math> be an open neighbourhood of <math>\overline{\Delta_k}</math> then <math>\bar{\partial}(\beta_k-\beta'_{k+1})=0</math> on <math>U_k</math> and we can apply again the Dolbeault-Grothendieck lemma to find a <math>(p,q-2)</math>-form <math>\gamma_k</math> such that <math> \beta_k-\beta'_{k+1}=\bar{\partial}\gamma_k</math> on <math>\Delta_k</math>. Now, let <math>V_k</math> be an [[open set]] with <math>\overline{\Delta_k} \subset V_k \subsetneq U_k</math> and <math>\rho_k: \Delta_\varepsilon^n(0)\to\R</math> a smooth function such that: 

:<math>\operatorname{supp}(\rho_k)\subset U_k, \qquad \rho|_{V_k}=1, \qquad \rho_k|_{\Delta_\varepsilon^n(0)\setminus U_k}=0.</math>

Then <math>\rho_k\gamma_k</math> is a well-defined smooth form on <math>\Delta_\varepsilon^n(0)</math> which satisfies 

:<math>\beta_k=\beta'_{k+1}+\bar{\partial}(\gamma_k\rho_k) \quad \text{on} \quad \Delta_{k},</math>

hence the form 

:<math>\beta_{k+1}:=\beta'_{k+1}+\bar{\partial}(\gamma_k\rho_k)</math> 

satisfies

:<math>\begin{align}
\beta_{k+1}|_{\Delta_k}  &=\beta'_{k+1}+\bar{\partial}\gamma_k=\beta_k\\
\bar{\partial}\beta_{k+1}&=\bar{\partial}\beta'_{k+1}=\alpha|_{\Delta_{k+1}}
\end{align}</math>

<u>Case 2.</u> If instead <math>\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\Complex^n}^{p,1}(U),</math> we cannot apply the Dolbeault-Grothendieck lemma twice; we take <math>\beta_i</math> and <math>\Delta_i</math> as before, we want to show that 

:<math>\left \| \left. \left ({\beta_i}_I-{\beta_{i+1}}_I \right ) \right |_{\Delta_{k-1}} \right \|_\infty<2^{-i}.</math>

Again, we proceed by induction on <math> i</math>: for <math> i=1</math> the answer is given by the Dolbeault-Grothendieck lemma. Next we suppose that the claim is true for <math> k>1</math>. We take <math> \Delta_{k+1}\supset\overline{\Delta_k}</math> such that <math>\Delta_{k+1}\cup\lbrace\Delta_i\rbrace_{i=1}^k</math> covers <math>\Delta_\varepsilon^n(0)</math>, then we can find a <math>(p,0)</math>-form <math>\beta'_{k+1}</math> such that 

:<math>\alpha|_{\Delta_{k+1}}=\bar{\partial}\beta'_{k+1},</math>

which also satisfies <math>\bar{\partial}(\beta_k-\beta'_{k+1})=0</math> on <math>\Delta_k</math>, i.e. <math>\beta_k-\beta'_{k+1}</math> is a holomorphic <math>(p,0)</math>-form wherever defined, hence by the [[Stone–Weierstrass theorem]] we can write it as

:<math>\beta_k-\beta'_{k+1}=\sum_{|I|=p}(P_I+r_I)dz_I</math>

where <math>P_I</math> are polynomials and 

:<math>\left \| r_I|_{\Delta_{k-1}} \right \|_\infty<2^{-k},</math> 

but then the form 

:<math> \beta_{k+1}:=\beta'_{k+1}+\sum_{|I|=p}P_Idz_I</math> 

satisfies

:<math>\begin{align}
\bar{\partial}\beta_{k+1}&=\bar{\partial}\beta'_{k+1}=\alpha|_{\Delta_{k+1}}\\
\left \| ({\beta_k}_I-{\beta_{k+1}}_I)|_{\Delta_{k-1}} \right \|_\infty&=\| r_I\|_\infty<2^{-k}
\end{align}</math>

which completes the induction step; therefore we have built a sequence <math>\lbrace\beta_i\rbrace_{i\in\N}</math> which uniformly converges to some <math>(p,0)</math>-form <math>\beta</math> such that <math>\alpha|_{\Delta_{\varepsilon}^n(0)}=\bar{\partial}\beta</math>. QED

==Dolbeault's theorem==
Dolbeault's theorem is a complex analog<ref>In contrast to de Rham cohomology, Dolbeault cohomology is no longer a topological invariant because it depends closely on complex structure.</ref> of [[de Rham's theorem]].  It asserts that the Dolbeault cohomology is isomorphic to the [[sheaf cohomology]] of the [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]] of holomorphic differential forms.  Specifically,

:<math>H^{p,q}(M)\cong H^q(M,\Omega^p)</math>

where <math>\Omega^p</math> is the sheaf of holomorphic ''p'' forms on ''M''. 

A version of the Dolbeault theorem also holds for Dolbeault cohomology with coefficients in a holomorphic vector bundle <math>E</math>. Namely one has an isomorphism

<math display="block">H^{p,q}(M,E) \cong H^q(M, \Omega^{p} \otimes E).</math>

A version for [[logarithmic form]]s has also been established.<ref>{{citation| last=Navarro Aznar|first= Vicente|title=Sur la théorie de Hodge–Deligne|year=1987|volume=90|issue=1|pages=11–76|journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]|doi=10.1007/bf01389031|bibcode= 1987InMat..90...11A|s2cid= 122772976}}, Section 8</ref>

===Proof===
Let <math>\mathcal{F}^{p,q}</math> be the [[fine sheaf]] of <math>C^{\infty}</math> forms of type <math>(p,q)</math>. Then the <math>\overline{\partial}</math>-Poincaré lemma says that the sequence

:<math>\Omega^{p,q} \xrightarrow{\overline{\partial}} \mathcal{F}^{p,q+1}\xrightarrow{\overline{\partial}} \mathcal{F}^{p,q+2} \xrightarrow{\overline{\partial}} \cdots </math>

is exact. Like any long [[exact sequence]], this sequence breaks up into short exact sequences. The long exact sequences of cohomology corresponding to these give the result, once one uses that the higher cohomologies of a fine sheaf vanish.

==Explicit example of calculation ==
The Dolbeault cohomology of the <math>n</math>-dimensional [[complex projective space]] is

:<math>H^{p,q}_{\bar{\partial}}(P^n_{\Complex})=\begin{cases}\Complex & p=q\\ 0 &\text{otherwise}\end{cases}</math>

We apply the following well-known fact from [[Hodge theory#Hodge theory for complex projective varieties|Hodge theory]]: 

:<math>H_{\rm dR}^k \left (P^n_{\Complex},\Complex \right )=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}_{\bar{\partial}}(P^n_{\Complex})</math> 

because <math>P^n_{\Complex}</math> is a compact [[Kähler manifold|Kähler complex manifold]]. Then <math>b_{2k+1}=0</math> and 

:<math>b_{2k}=h^{k,k}+\sum_{p+q=2k,p\ne q}h^{p,q}=1.</math>

Furthermore we know that <math>P^n_{\Complex}</math> is Kähler, and <math>0\ne[\omega^k]\in H^{k,k}_{\bar{\partial}}(P^n_{\Complex}),</math> where <math>\omega</math> is the fundamental form associated to the [[Fubini–Study metric]] (which is indeed Kähler), therefore <math>h^{k,k}=1</math> and <math>h^{p,q}=0</math> whenever <math>p\ne q,</math> which yields the result.
